speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 8 I informed the house that I had accepted President Kennedy's invitation to visit Washington on February 20.
Detailed arrangements have now been made for that visit. I shall be accompanied by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the ambassador in Washington. I understand that the President will be accompanied by the secretary of state, Mr. Dean Rusk, and by the United States ambassador designate to Canada, Mr. Livingstone Merchant, whose recent appointment evoked universal approval everywhere in our country.
I wish to take this opportunity to express again my satisfaction at the prospect of a private and informal meeting with the President. I feel certain that at this time of serious risk in international affairs all members of the house will agree that it is beneficial that there should be discussion between the leaders of the United States and Canadian governments.
I shall not be able to specify in advance or in detail any of the subjects for discussion. Naturally among those subjects will be the most critical international issues of the moment, and I hope it will also be possible to cover other international matters and the general field of United States-Canadian relations.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will have listened with interest to the further information from the Prime Minister about his visit to Washington. I think we all agree with him that it is important and is bound to be beneficial to have these talks, particularly at this time.
I can only repeat what I said the other day. We on this side wish him every success in these talks and in the effort which they symbolize to improve the already good relations between our two countries. May I say that I learned with particular pleasure from the Prime Minister that one of the United States participants will be Mr. Livingstone Merchant. I am sure everyone, as the Prime Minister has said, welcomes him back to Canada where he has already been stationed, and where he has already done fine service in the cause of good relations between our two countries.
May I presume to suggest to the Prime Minister that one of the things of value that might emanate from these talks would be a reaffirmation on the part of both governments of their strong support for the Secretary General of the United Nations, who is now under such a vicious and unjustifiable attack.

Mr. Speaker, the members of this group wish the Prime Minister every success in his talks with President Kennedy working toward world peace and disarmament and the other policies that all of us in the house hope will develop in the months and years ahead. We trust that in doing so he will present what I think is the view of all the Canadian people by putting forward a constructive, co-operative but truly Canadian policy that represents our status as a nation.

Mr. Speaker, I thank both hon. gentlemen. May I say to the Leader of the Opposition that a reiteration of the attitude of Canadians as a whole respecting Mr. Hammerskjold and his contribution to world peace will certainly be in order and will be one of the first things to be discussed. All of us are agreed that the United Nations shall not be destroyed as a result of the truculent attitude of any one nation; nor shall it become, as the U.S.S.R. would have it become if Mr. Khrushchev's words of last September mean anything, a puppet of the U.S.S.R.

speechtext:
1.	Do any regulations exist with respect to the admission of workers from the United States to Canada for employment in the construction of pipelines in British Columbia?

3.	Have any American workers been admitted to Canada, since January 1960, for such work and pursuant to these regulations?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minisier of Citizenship and Immigration):
maintopic: U.S. PIPE LINE WORKERS, B.C.  REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to question 1 is yes. The answer to question 2 is as follows. Section 7 (l)(h) of the Immigration Act provides that persons engaged in a legitimate profession, trade or occupation may be allowed to enter and remain in Canada as non-immigrants for the temporary exercise of their respective callings. It is the government's policy that such persons shall not be admitted unless the examining immigration officer is satisfied that the individual's services are required in

Canada. In the case of such trades and occupations as pipe-line workers, where it is considered that the employment of a permanent resident may be adversely affected, the national employment service is consulted to ensure that the services of local residents with the required qualifications are not available. Admission of workers from the United States for temporary employment in the construction of pipe lines in British Columbia is governed by this section and the policy I have outlined.
The answer to question 3 is yes.
The answer to question 4 is that 17 persons have been admitted to Canada from the United States since January, 1960, for temporary employment in the construction of pipe lines in British Columbia. Five of these were described as superintendents, one of an entire project, with an assistant, and the others of various phases of the operation; three were engineers and three were foremen, all with specialized functions; there were two office managers, a project manager and a chief inspector. One was described as a material co-ordinator and the last was a representative of the United States concern interested in the purchase of the gas from the Canadian owners. All of these men except one foreman, who has since been admitted to Canada for permanent residence, and the representative of the United States purchasers, were destined for employment to one or other of the two concerns who are engineering and constructing the pipe line in the Cranbrook area. Temporary admission was allowed for various periods of time up to a year, pending completion of the project, and in each case the approval of the national employment service was obtained.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext: I ask leave to move the adjournment of the house under standing order No. 26 for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely the addition of 165,000 persons to the ranks of the unemployed during 'he past month.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
The hon. member for Essex East has invoked standing order No. 26 to ask for leave to move the adjournment of the house to discuss an increase in the number of persons unemployed.
No one would question that the matter is one of public importance. What I have to determine is whether there is that urgency of debate in connection with this matter which would warrant our interrupting the normal course of our proceedings so as to permit a debate on this subject matter on the ground that there has not been, or is not, an opportunity, or sufficient opportunity, for the house to discuss this question. It seems to me that is the simple proposition before the Chair.
Similar motions have been moved in the past, or at least leave has been requested in the past, and I have on each occasion taken the view that to discuss unemployment in general terms under a motion to adjourn the house under standing order 26, where there has been ample discussion or considerable discussion, or at least ample opportunity in general debates to discuss the question of unemployment, would not be in accordance with the urgency of debate which the rule contemplates, and I see no reason for taking a different course at this time, more particularly as we have had very considerable discussion of the serious problem of unemployment both in the immediately preceding days
Unemployment
and in the earlier part of the session. Moreover, I expect there will be ample opportunity in the ensuing days.
If the hon. member for Essex East has a word to say on the question of urgency of debate I will hear him on that subject only.

subsubtopic: MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I think Your Honour's statement of the procedural situation is one which will be accepted by all hon. members. We are not asking that there should be a general discussion of the problem. As you have pointed out, there has already been presented this session an opportunity for discussing the generality of the problem. What we are asking is an opportunity to discuss something new, namely the fact that the government's announcement today indicates that 165,000 more persons are out of work than in the previous reporting period.
This is a new fact, and if we are not given an opportunity to debate this matter at this time there will be no opportunity provided in the foreseeable future. The estimates of the Department of Labour have not been called. If they had been called, we might have urged the government to introduce those estimates forthwith. But there is nothing now before the house which would enable us under our procedures to discuss this matter which, as Your Honour said, no one will suggest is not a matter of urgent public importance.
This question has suddenly confronted us in its present serious proportions; and, because of its admitted character, it would seem to me that Your Honour would, on reflection, agree that there being no opportunity today, no opportunity that is presented unless the Department of Labour esimates were before us, we should not be precluded at this time from discussing this further development which arises out of the most important domestic problem which, regrettably, faces our country today. For these reasons I ask leave to present this motion.

should like to direct a question to the Minister of Finance. Has the minister noticed the question asked the Prime Minister on Monday last with respect to whether consultations were held recently between the government and the Bank of Canada concerning the recent sale by the bank of unusually large amounts of bonds and securities, thereby reducing the available money supply in Canada, and the reply of the Prime Minister that an answer would be forthcoming at the earliest possible time? Would the minister enlighten the country as to why there is a contraction of the money supply at a time of growing unemployment?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have already been on my feet three times today attempting to answer this question so that the hon. member might not be put to the trouble of asking it again. I was made aware of the question which he asked on Monday in my absence and to which the Prime Minister indicated an answer would be made.
It is normal in this country for the money supply to contract in the month of January. In that month the Bank of Canada normally reduces its holdings of government securities in order to offset the effect on chartered bank cash reserves of the heavy post-Christmas seasonal flow-back of currency from the general public into the chartered banks.
The hon. member has added to his question an indication that what has been happening has unusually reduced the available money supply in Canada. I should like to point out


to him, Mr. Speaker, that the total money supply, which includes currency in the hands of the public as well as total chartered bank deposits, on December 28, 1960 was 5.2 per cent greater than it had been 52 weeks earlier. As of February 1, 1961 the 52-week increase, that is the increase over the same date 52 weeks earlier, was 5.5 per cent.
Perhaps I might add some figures in this respect. The total money supply in Canada on February 1, 1961 was $13,763 million, and this was an increase of $718 million over the corresponding date in 1960.
I should like to ask a supplementary question. Would the minister admit that the sales of bonds and securities by the Bank of Canada exceed normal sales for the same month in other years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will not admit what is not a fact, namely that there has been any abnormal decrease in the money supply. The actual decrease that occurred in January was confined to the weeks in which January 11 and January 18 fell, and there was an increase from January 18 to January 25 and another increase between January 25 and February 1 in the total money supply.

I should like to ask a supplementary question. In his answer the minister has given figures relating the present money supply to the money supply 12 months earlier. He will be aware that the money supply 18 months and two years ago was approximately at the same figure as it is today. Would he explain why there has not been an increase in the money supply comparable to the increase in the gross national product, which would be about 4 per cent in that period, and the increase in population of perhaps 3 per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member must be well aware that parliament has confided to the Bank of Canada full authority over questions pertaining to money supply. The government has no authority in the field of monetary policy.
It has responsibility.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the hon. member has overlooked certain facts. The money supply in recent months has reached an all-time record, and when he speaks of the money supply of 18 months ago or two years ago may I point out that at that time it did not reach the figure that it has reached latterly.
Very close. About the same.

I point out that the money supply on December 28, 1960 reached a figure of $13,811 million, which was $687 million more than the figure 12 months earlier. I pointed out that the increase at February 1 over the same date a year ago was $718 million.
I referred to two years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to add, if I may, to the answer I gave the hon. member for Port Arthur. I would like to give the reasons it was considered impracticable for Canadian Car Company Limited to carry out the next phase of the Bobcat program at their Fort William plant.
(1)	The company has spent approximately $21 million in establishing an up-to-date and modern facility in the Montreal area.
LMr. Speaker.]

(2)	All engineering and design personnel are located at the Montreal plant.
(3)	The testing facilities of the army, which will be required to be used during the preproduction pilot stage of the program, are located on the Montreal road outside of Ottawa en route to Montreal.
(4)	Personnel of the Canadian army development establishment and other members of the quartermaster general's branch, who will be required to exercise very close supervision of the program, are located at army headquarters in Ottawa.
(5)	The senior officers of the company who are directly concerned with this program are located in Montreal and could not be transferred to Fort William.
Following the 20 preproduction pilot models being produced, when it is possible to proceed with the production of the balance of 480 vehicles this will be determined on the basis of competitive tender. This could mean that if Canadian Car Company Limited were the successful tenderer, production of the Bobcat could take place at Fort William, provided the company so elected. However-and I want to be frank in this connection-it is extremely doubtful whether the company would be in a competitive position if the manufacture took place at Fort William.
We have given a great deal of attention to this matter and have endeavoured in every way possible to do our part to assure the maintenance of the program, but the circumstances of distance and of non-competibil-ity, and the other circumstances to which I have made reference, determine the course in question in so far as the preproduction program is concerned.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to remark how satisfactory it has been to have the annual report of the Canada Council before the public accounts committee. I wish to compliment the members of that committee, of which I am not ordinarily a member, for the way they have approached this matter, and the chairman for his work.
I did want to pay a tribute to the man who headed the Canada Council and who has since died. He was a man I did not know personally. The Hon. Brooke Claxton made a great impression on those of us who had not known him before and certainly the feeling I have to a much greater extent than I had before is that the Canada Council is an expression of one of his dreams and ambitions. He is now gone, but I hope we can all continue to see in the Canada Council the kind of Canadianism and Canadian idea he was out to express.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORT TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE

I do not desire to hold up this motion, but this gives me an opportunity to pay my tribute to the work of the council and especially to the contribution made to that work by the late chairman and my former colleague in the house, Mr. Brooke Claxton. In doing this may I add my expression of good will to the present chairman.
I was interested to read in the press not long ago that the present chairman had indicated that more funds would be required if the council is to be able to carry out the kind of job it hopes to perform. No doubt this is one of the matters which will be considered by those concerned, and at this time I have nothing to say about that request. However, I do feel, as I am sure all hon. members feel, that the council has already abundantly justified its existence. We hope it will be able to continue that existence in a way which will make a special contribution to the development of Canada in fields other than material.

subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORT TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Before this motion passes I should just like to express my appreciation of the work which has been done by the Canada Council since its formation during, shall I say, what was almost an experimental period, because many problems had to be met.
I rise principally to urge that every consideration should be given to groups in the smaller communities such as little theatres and others connected with various forms of the arts and to suggest that there might possibly be some total survey made of the needs of these smaller communities across Canada. I personally am a great believer in doing even more in percentage terms for the smaller communities than is done in the cities where the opportunities are so much greater. I firmly believe that if the council can make a grant for someone to study constitutional law which I do not look upon as a cultural activity-indeed, I was rather surprised that such a grant should have been made-then, surely, the council could do something for the smaller communities which I represent.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REFERENCE OF REPORT TO PUBLIC ACCOUNTS COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I thank the hon. gentlemen who have participated in this short but, I think, effective debate. It indicates the unanimity of hon. members in this house with regard to the necessity of encouraging those concerned with Canada's cultural and artistic standards.
Mention was made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) of the request made recently by the chairman of the Canada Council, Dr. Bissell, who, I know, will be a worthy successor to the Hon. Brooke Claxton. Dr. Bissell and those associated with him made a presentation to the government in connection with the needs of the council and stated in relation to the scholarship and fellowship program, and to the organization representing the country's developing arts, that certain minimal additional sums would be required to meet the present needs in both these fields. With regard to the scholarships and fellowships, the request was for an additional $250,000. In addition to that, for organizations such as were referred to by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and other artistic organizations across Canada, a further $250,000 would be required.
The income from the endowment fund for the current fiscal year is estimated to be approximately $2,900,000, and those associated with the board estimate that a further $500,000 would be required. The need of assistance for the cultural things of life are indicated by the fact that the board's representations were to the effect that in 1957-58 90205-6-131J
Public Accounts
Canada's theatres asked for $89,000 and were granted $60,000; in 1960-61 they asked for $290,000 and were given $119,000. In connection with orchestras in various parts of Canada, in 1957-58 ten Canadian orchestras asked for $172,000 and were granted $130,000; in 1960-61 nine orchestras asked for $245,000 and were granted $205,000. In so far as the smaller communities are concerned, there are some seven or eight orchestras in such communities which need help, help which cannot now be given because grants to orchestras at the present level already account for over one fifth of the funds available for all artistic organizations.
Finally, in the field of ballet, in 1957-58 the grant asked for was $136,000 and the amount granted was just $6,000 less, while in 196061 the amount asked for was $225,000 and the amount granted was $160,000.
Believing, as all of us do, that there is a major need for the encouragement of the arts, humanities and social sciences in Canada -a need to stimulate the national culture- I have no doubt these are matters which will receive, and can receive, the attention of the committee to which this report will go if the present motion is passed.
May I conclude by saying that I join with the hon. member from Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) and the Leader of the Opposition in their references to the late Brooke Claxton. He made an outstanding contribution, first in the days of war, then in the parliament of this country and, later, upon ceasing to be a member of parliament and of the cabinet of Mr. St. Laurent, by giving leadership to the arts, something that is most laudable and commendable. I appreciate the attitude taken by members in all parts of the house and trust that when the report of the Canada Council comes before the committee the commendation to the late chairman and the manner in which the council was conducted last year will be representative of what will happen again this year.

Mr. Speaker, I should have thought the point was so very plain that it would not indeed have been raised. This is a motion in the time honoured form. It has become practically an annual motion; the form of it was changed only after the Canada Council was brought into being and was enlarged simply to include, as the present motion does, the accounts and the financial statements of the Canada Council and the report of the Auditor General thereon.
What is attempted in the present amendment is to introduce something quite different and quite outside the scope of the motion. The motion contemplates a reference to the public accounts committee of certain specified documents. First, there are the two volumes of the public accounts for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1960 and, second, the report of the Auditor General thereon. Third, there are the financial statements of the Canada Council and, fourth, the report of the Auditor General thereon.
That does not open the door for any hon. member to tack on the motion everything that occurs to him might well be considered by this committee. That would be opening the door to importing into such a motion matter that is entirely foreign to the motion. The public accounts committee can have referred to it many matters but a motion of this kind does not open the way for hon. members to

add to the motion everything that it may appear to them desirable to have considered by the public accounts committee.
I point out, Mr. Speaker, that there has been no little misapprehension indicated already in this matter. The Bank of Canada does not make an annual report. It is the governor of the Bank of Canada who makes a report and, so far as audit is concerned, the auditor general has no function whatsoever with respect to the Bank of Canada. Parliament's own legislation has provided for the appointment of auditors to the Bank of Canada. The power is given to the governor in council to appoint auditors for the Bank of Canada annually. The provisions of the legislation are quite specific on that point. The public accounts do not include the report of the Bank of Canada at all. It is a quite separate report and it comes to the minister annually about the middle of March. So, Mr. Speaker, the amendment purports to deal with something that is very different in nature from the documents that are specifically referred in the motion itself and are proposed to be referred to the committee.
I began, Mr. Speaker, by referring to the fact that this is a traditional motion. I do not recall any previous occasion when the motion was even debated. It has always been in this standard form. Normally it is the desire of all hon. members to have the public accounts and the report of the Auditor General thereon referred to the committee, and it seems to me that the discussion that has taken place this afternoon has just been a way of planting in the minds of hon. members the idea that such a motion can be amended by dragging into it anything that an hon. member thinks appropriate to refer to the committee, and in my respectful submission that is certainly not within the procedure of the house.

Resolved,-That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Customs Tariff and to provide:
1.	That the said act be amended by adding thereto immediately after section 2 thereof the following section:
"2A. (1) For the purposes of this act, goods shall be deemed to be of a class or kind made or produced in Canada if
(a)	in the case of goods other than goods custom-made to specifications, goods of approximately the same class or kind are made or produced in Canada; and
(b)	in the case of goods custom-made to specifications, adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time.
(2)	Notwithstanding subsection (1), goods other than goods custom-made to specifications shall be deemed not to be of a class or kind made or produced in Canada unless at least ten per cent of the normal Canadian consumption of goods of the same or approximately the same class or kind are made or produced in Canada.
(3)	The decision of the minister shall be final with respect to the following matters:
(a)	the normal Canadian consumption of the goods described in subsection (2), and
(b)	whether goods are custom-made to specifications, and whether adequate facilities exist in Canada for the economic production of such goods within a reasonable period of time."
2.	That subsections (9) and (10) of section 6 of the said act be repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"(9) For the purposes of this act, notwithstanding section 2A, goods may be deemed to be of a class or kind not made or produced in Canada where similar goods made or produced in Canada are not offered for sale to the ordinary agencies of wholesale or retail distribution or are not offered to all purchasers on equal terms under like conditions, having regard to the custom and usage of trade."
3.	That subsection (4) of section 6A of the said act be repealed.
4.	That any enactment founded upon this resolution shall be deemed to have come into force on the 21st day of December, 1960, and to have applied to all goods mentioned therein imported or taken out of warehouse for consumption on or after that day, and to have applied to goods previously imported for which no entry for consumption was made before that day.

Mr. Chairman, it is more than a week since we last discussed this resolution. I know that in the interval the Minister of Finance has made a very brief trip to western Canada. I rather thought that with the introduction of this resolution again he might come forward with some amendment to his proposals because I am sure while he was out there he heard a considerable amount of indignation expressed with respect to the arbitrary powers being taken by the ministry under the proposed legislation, the elimination of appeals to the tariff board and to higher courts, which practice has been in effect for years, and so on.
I certainly know that the interval has been a fortunate one as far as the public are concerned because since we last discussed the matter it has become very apparent that

Customs Tariff
there is widespread apprehension in the country as was expressed by members of the opposition when the resolution was introduced. As I recall, hitherto in our discussion of this subject the debate has centred on two matters, neither of which I propose to deal with at this stage although I will certainly raise my voice with respect to them at later stages of the debate.
I refer first of all to the question of arbitrary power and the elimination of appeals to the tariff board and, second, the adverse effect that these proposals will have, particularly with regard to machinery, on other producers, on manufacturers, on end users and the effect it will have on efficiency if something less than the best machine proves prohibitively expensive for the people whom we are trying to encourage to get into production so efficiently that they will be able to meet the exceedingly keen competition of the world and enlarge our exports. As I say, I am not going to deal with those two matters at this time.
I want to remind hon. members that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue put very much foremost in their arguments the point that there is nothing really new in this legislation except that it will result in a return to the law with respect to the administration of the "class or kind" provisions that was operative prior to 1950, a decade ago. It is very flattering to have the new administration suggest that they have no new principles to offer with respect to this form of customs administration and that they admire and are returning to the practices of the Mackenzie King government and the Liberal principles with respect to customs that were operative prior to what they call the erosion which they say has taken place in the last ten years.
So far as that rather bland form of approach to this debate is concerned, I want to say that it has no foundation in fact whatsoever. I think I can demonstrate that both ministers are exceedingly naive if they think they can spoof the House of Commons, even members of their own party from areas where exports are vital, into thinking that this is simply an innocent return to a long time practice, a practice that was particularly typical and had the endorsation of the Liberal party which is known to be a party that is anxious to expand trade.
The other assertion with which I should like to deal and which I think is equally naive is that our partners in GATT will accept the minister's proposals in this legislation as nothing new or of much consequence to them, but merely a return to the situation which was in effect in Canada with respect to customs administration when the GATT agreement was originally signed in 1947.

I should like to direct the attention of the committee to the interpretation that the two ministers have given that the decisions of the tariff board in the decade create an erosion. I think it was the Minister of National Revenue who had this to say in the course of the debate-this is the type of approach that I do not believe they expect the opposition to accept, nor is it going to salve the conscience of their own supporters who would be horrified if they really studied this proposition and realized some of the implications that will flow from it in the matter of stifling trade and that will affect their constituencies in western Canada, the maritimes and other areas. I said there was a straightforward claim that this was a return to Liberal tariff doctrine. I should like to quote from the remarks of the Minister of National Revenue as recorded on page 1688 of Hansard for February 2, 1961:
We are not going back to the days of R. B. Bennett; we are simply going back to the practices which were pursued, and I think properly so, by the government of Mr. Mackenzie King, and those associated with him up until at least 1950.
I want to establish, and I think I can very clearly the rather substantial difference with respect to some facts that I will give as to the legal decisions that have been given in the last 10 years in tariff board decisions, and the very inaccurate, rather casual interpretations that were given by both ministers in the course of the debate so far. I hope members of the government party who are not sympathetic to high tariffs will note these remarks with care.
I should like to refer particularly to the shovel case which both ministers emphasized, and I think properly so, because the case with respect to the dipper size of the shovels was perhaps the one that received the greatest amount of attention in litigation during the past 10 years. There were two appeals one of which went to the exchequer court and to the supreme court. These ministers are trying to convince their followers and the country that the final result was a judgment that was contrary to the practices and to the decisions of the tariff board as they existed some 10 years earlier.
In order to indicate the rather casual way in which this matter has been presented to the committee I should like to refer to page 1698 of Hansard for February 2, 1961. In so far as the shovel case is concerned, the Minister of Finance did not think this was worth going into in very much detail. He shrugged his shoulders and said that all members of the committee would understand how petty it is to suggest, as the tariff board did, that a

shovel of 2.5 cubic yard capacity is not made in Canada and the maximum size of shovel made in Canada is two cubic yards, the tariff board was being unduly restrictive in that interpretation.
The minister did refer to one appeal, appeal No. 306, but inadvertently or otherwise it is a great surprise to me to find that no reference whatever was made by either minister when they were reviewing this so-called erosion to the original and basic appeal with respect to shovels, which was appeal No. 272. The tariff board, in appeal No. 272, came to this conclusion:
The obvious purpose of tariff item 427a-
This 427a is an item in the tariff which was inserted by the Liberal administration for the purpose of establishing that if goods of a class or kind, of iron and steel and they are mostly machinery items, were not in fact being made in Canada, the importer of those articles would not be obliged to pay the 22J per cent most favoured nation rate but, on the contrary, would be allowed to have machinery that was the most efficient and suitable without the burden of a high tariff and would pay a low tariff of 7.5 per cent if imported from the United States or free if imported from the United Kingdom.
The tariff board report states this:
From the standpoint of the user, domestic machinery is not "available" unless such domestic machinery is precisely suitable for the purposes he has in mind. On the other hand, it would deprive the domestic manufacturer of the protection to which he is reasonably entitled were he required to supply a more or less precise duplicate of a particular foreign machine in order to take the latter machine out of tariff item 427a.
The correct interpretation of these two items would appear to require, therefore, the exploration of a middle ground between two impractical extremes, in which connection it is of assistance to ponder again the wording of section 6 (10) of the Customs Tariff Act, as set out earlier herein.
This is the section which is now before us for elimination.
When subsection 10 is read with the wording of tariff item 427a in mind, it is clear that the word "quantities" as used therein would appear to contemplate a counting of pieces of machinery. That being so, it must follow that the subsection contemplates further the counting of pieces of machinery of sufficient similarity, the one to the other, to make the exercise in arithmetic at least a matter of common sense. Similarity sufficient in degree to make sense of the counting must presuppose a reasonable degree of narrowness in the grouping or classification. Therefore, reading subsection (10) along with tariff item 427a, it would seem obvious that the classifications contemplated under the latter must be sufficiently narrow to give to subsection (10) reasonable meaning and effect. Contrariwise, the very broad classification of the tariff item contended for by the appellant would reduce this parallel section of the same act to an absurdity-apart altogether from which, his proposition as advanced does not commend itself as a sensible and practical basis for classification of "all machinery . . . not otherwise provided." 90205-6-132

What was the result of that decision? Did that decision upset what the administration had invoked? Was there erosion of the decision of the customs department and the deputy minister? Did it run counter to made in Canada orders that had been standing with respect to these items for quite a number of years? Is this typical of the erosion that hon. members say has taken place?
On the contrary, the tariff board confirmed the ruling of the administration. The department had itself, as it does all the time, made inquiries as to what types of shovels were in fact being made in Canada and what shovels of other dimensions were not being made in Canada. In a regular way the department issued to the trade their periodic declarations as to what machinery would bear the made in Canada rate, which is high, and what imports would bear the not made in Canada rate, which is relatively low.
This is very clear. Not within the last ten years, but prior to that there was this declaration by the department itself that shovels of a size in excess of two cubic yards were not in fact being made in Canada, and on that occasion the tariff board simply confirmed what the administration said was the fact.
There was no erosion there. But what happened? I think this decision on appeal No. 272 was rendered in about March of 1953. Very shortly afterward the administration was persuaded to issue a new order with respect to what shovels were made in Canada and what shovels were not made in Canada. We had another one in 1948, which said that power lawn mowers had been transferred from the category of a class or kind not made in Canada to that of a class or kind made in Canada provided they had a cut of from 18 inches to 30 inches inclusive.
At about the time of GATT in 1947 we had one saying that foundry jolt squeeze moulding machines, 10-inch and 12-inch sizes, had been transferred from the category of a class or kind not made in Canada to that

of a class or kind made in Canada. Is this taking in the whole class? Is this the type of ruling the minister said was made under the Liberal administration under whose name and reputation in trade matters he is now attempting to sell this particular legislation?
I referred earlier to Mr. H. D. Scully. This refers to the shovel case. I did not have at my fingertips the actual reference to the testimony Mr. Scully gave in that case but I have it now. Mr. Scully's statements are recorded from pages 367 to 371 of the appeal with respect to case No. 272. Mr. Scully said:
These rulings have been in effect now for some 17 years. We were at great pains, as I say, to investigate, and had we ruled at the time on the basis of all earth moving or rock movement or equipment of the nature that is under consideration, or had we ruled in accordance with the total amount imported in any one year or produced in any one year in Canada-had we ruled on that basis, the company would not have got the ruling they did-
Because they needed a ruling under present law that 10 per cent of the consumption in Canada was in fact of a class or kind of article made in Canada. He went on to say:
The minister, as I say, was most meticulous and we were trying to do the best we could under the circumstances and we had to narrow the sizes and types of shovels that were made at that time in order to qualify under the law at all.
This was to the advantage of the appellant. This type of thing has not disappeared. Trade and industry are similar today to what they were a decade ago and more. We have emphasized the importance to an industry starting up to operate efficiently, getting the best possible equipment; and particularly if the consumption in Canada is not to the extent of 10 per cent of our requirements, an importer of machinery and articles of that type going into production and manufacturing should not have an undue burden of tariff placed upon his operations.
We had a case in 1960, under the present administration; I refer to appeal No. 450. I think this is indicative of the type of problem that we feel is worthy of attention by members of the government who I am sure are anxious to see industry get going and not have a burden placed upon it at the start that will make it inefficient either to the extent of having to put out a higher price to the Canadian end user or have costs established for them by the original tariff which would make it impossible to compete in outside markets.
This appeal was heard by the new tariff board, the personnel of which I believe were not members of the board at the time the other decision was made that I have referred to. The decision was given on September 12, 1960. The argument here was whether a horizontal vacuum tilting pan filter was of a
Customs Tariff
class or kind of filter within the meaning of item 427a; in other words, not made in Canada. It was agreed that tilting pan filters were not made in Canada. We have a new government in office, and here the department seems to be arguing the other way. I quote from the judgment:
However, counsel for the department adduced evidence relating to a Dorr-Oliver-Long scroll discharge filter of Canadian manufacture and submitted that, while not identical with the pan filter, it was similar to it and therefore was of the same class or kind.
This is under the new administration. The officials now took the other side of the argument in a case of this kind and they are met with an appeal by the importer. What did the brand new board decide in 1960 in connection with this case? I read from the judgment:
The appellant, which operates both scroll type horizontal filters and tilting pan filters, in one particular process, in various locations, gave evidence that the efficiency of the pan filter for their particular operation was much greater and that its considerable additional costs could quite easily be recovered from savings in the first year's operation.
The decision was:
The imported tilting pan filter differs substantially from the scroll discharge filter in design, in method of operation, in cost, in principal use and efficiency in certain uses. On the evidence adduced in this appeal the board finds that they are not of the same class or kind.
I ask the committee whether, in this loosely drawn legislation before us, we would get a decision such as this from the minister? This is not a shelf goods item; this is perhaps a made to order item. What is the minister going to do? Here is a producer who has made up his mind that this one type of filter is so efficient that he could recover from savings in the first year's operation the additional cost in connection with it. It was a more expensive filter than the Canadian made filter. To be efficient this is what he wanted. Under the new law, what is the minister going to do? Is he going to say that, using the word "approximately" and taking advantage of the personal discretion that is given to him alone-his decision is no longer going to be appealable to the tariff board-the official's contention was right? What is his decision going to be in a situation such as I have outlined in this recent case where, very fortunately, I think, for efficiency in production, the new members of the tariff board appointed by this administration interpret the law in the same way as I have indicated it was interpreted for years. There was a very definite distinction arrived at. They said that it was not necessarily one of size.

Customs Tariff
In answer to the question raised by the hon. member for Medicine Hat earlier, may I say it does not always have to be determined by dimension or size. In the particular case to which I have reference the board said that on the evidence adduced the filter differed substantially in principal use, efficiency, method of operation, design, and so on. Here the department intended to tell this importer that he could not have this efficient machine; that he had to take something that was second best. I assume that under the new law there will be no appeal; there will be no necessity to look at decisions and results. Nobody in the country will know the precedents. This is the kind of thing that will be coming forward. Our people will be denied information or appeal and I do not see how this is going to help secondary industry in the country to become efficient.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: A frightful travesty of the facts.

I rise to make a few short remarks, and I hope they will be my last remarks on this particular amendment. I rise as the result of the remarks made by the Minister of Finance on February 3, at page 1729 of Hansard, in which he said that my particular speech:
-was just about as inimical to the interests of labour in Canada as I suppose any speech that any of us has heard in this chamber for a very long time.
I must say that I was rather flattered by the fact that the minister took such great note of what I had to say. In the few weeks I have been here I rather suspected there was a kind of social system here whereby those of us in the back reaches of the chamber were not particularly of any interest to those who were on the government front benches. But none the less, I was particularly horrified by what the minister said because I had a great deal of admiration for the Minister of Finance, knowing his high sense of proportion and his love of accuracy and as a man who was a member of the legal profession and was in a position tp evaluate evidence. However, when I came to read his speech I was very concerned because he accused me of talking as though this legislation were the expression of a high tariff policy. I refer hon. members to page 1729 of Hansard. 'What did I say at page 1711 of Hansard? Let me quote again:
1 suggest that the proposed amendment, though not one which may immediately bring about higher tariff policies, is none the less an open door toward future higher tariffs.
What I was suggesting was that there was a trend, a possibility that in the future this
[Mr. Benidickson.l
trend would continue. I expressed my concern not so much with this particular amendment. I am sure the minister has read my speech now and he will realize I was not expressing my concern as much with this amendment as with what had been said both on the part of the minister in his exchanges with the hon. member for Laurier and also on the part of his supporters in introducing a note of confusion that this was indeed a high tariff policy to protect Canadian industry.
Perhaps more than anything else I was appalled by the expressions of the opinion that really the only concern labour had was for high tariffs. I quoted from two documents which had been issued very recently and the minister himself indicated that he could remember a conference two years ago when this was not the case. I can only submit at this time that there has been a great deal of re-thinking of the whole tariff question as to high tariffs and low tariffs and not all of that thinking has been in the direction of high tariffs.
Possibly the minister now has on his desk some communications from labour organizations in which high tariffs are demanded. I would certainly hope so. I would expect there would perhaps be a few who might think differently but I am suggesting that the trend in the case of the majority is away from high tariffs, and I hope the minister will take notice of this fact.
I was particularly disturbed by the intemperate remarks regarding the ability of the present member for Peterborough to express the views of his constituents. I do not think we are here to rehash by-elections, and I will only say that I have expressed the same opinions in the house as I expressed on the hustings and that as far as I know these are the opinions of those who cast their votes on my behalf. I might say that the party represented by the minister lost half of its votes in that particular by-election in spite of having the best possible candidate and therefore I do not think his opinions necessarily reflect the views of the people of the constituency any more than mine do.
As found on page 1730 of Hansard, the minister made another misquotation when he said:
Here we have an hon. member saying that dumping may be a legitimate trade practice.
Of course, I said nothing of the kind. As found on page 1712 what I actually said was:
-what we call dumping may be regarded as a legitimate trade practice of the nation... on the other side of the fence.
That is not the same as saying that I am in favour of dumping or that I do not recognize

there is a definite difference between legitimate trade practices and dumping.
In the very few minutes I have I can only repeat what I said before. My opposition is based on the fact that this amendment could possibly restrict trade, that this may be indeed a great national policy as our newspapers and magazines are suggesting, and that no realistic appraisal of our tariff structure would indicate that higher tariffs are needed. However, if this re-definition of class or kind made in Canada is going to bring about more employment, I am extremely happy to hear it and before the debate is over I hope the minister will stand up and on the basis of his no doubt considerable degree of knowledge of my constituency indicate how reclassification will help employment in the Peterborough area. I know that the people of that area would be very happy to hear this. We have heard a great deal about shovels and .22 rifles. I am afraid these items do not have very much impact as far as employment is concerned in this constituency. Therefore I hope that before long the minister will rise and indicate in some way exactly how this reclassification will help this particular situation.

May I
ask the hon. member a question? Does the hon. member for Peterborough agree with the leader of his party in the house that they are for freer trade at the present time?
I do not know that he has said free trade-

Freer
trade.
As a long term objective, yes. I think freer trade is what we all must have, not only in Canada but throughout the world.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
No, sir.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Talk it out again.

As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to raise a question of privilege but I do intend to draw attention to the attitude toward the opposition expressed by the Minister of Finance from his seat just now.
From his seat.

We on the opposition side have sought to deal with the facts and to bring the facts to bear upon the legislation but from the government side we have heard nothing but personal attacks and vituperation since the debate began.
Customs Tariff

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not a statement of fact.

All the minister has to say is, "Here we go again". I must say it is about time the minister came back to this side of the house where he is evidently at home. He does not seem to realize that the meaning of the word "minister" is "servant", that he is the servant of this house and not its master and that it is about time this sort of thing stopped.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Hamilton South wishes to raise a point of order.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that the Minister of Finance does not have to sit here and take lectures from the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. We are discussing an item of legislation and it is a well known practice that the hon. member should not take up time in this way.

The hon. member, for whom I have the greatest possible respect, is entitled to his opinion, and I will abide by any rulings of the Chair. I could have said that this was a question of privilege. I do not intend to pursue this line any further although I must say that on the point of order I was very tempted to quote some precedents from a speech by the Minister of Finance in 1955 when he was over here, to which I may say no exception was taken by anyone on the treasury benches at that time. The members on the treasury benches at that time sought to reply to arguments that were made by the opposition and not to attack members of the opposition for daring to speak in the house. That is one of the differences.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. gentleman should smile when he says that.

If it will please the hon. member for Carleton I will be very glad to smile. It is something I have never found very hard to do. I have been trying to set a good example to the Minister of Finance for a long time but it does not seem to have taken.
I wish to say something about the statement that was made first by the Minister of National Revenue and repeated by the Minister of Finance on February 2, and which is found at page 1669 of Hansard. It reads as follows:
-we heard the hon. member-
That is myself.
-say that the present legislation apparently had some sinister connection with the legislation of 1958.

Customs Tariff
The reference is to the amendments to sections 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40, 40A and 40B of the Customs Act.
The legislation of 1958 was very good legislation and as was pointed out at that time it was badly needed for the purpose of making known to some foreign producers who were in the habit of exporting into Canada that they would not be permitted to do so on a basis of dumping in Canada. So salutary has been the effect of the mere enactment of that legislation that it has not been necessary once in the two and a half intervening years to apply that legislation in any particular case. The Minister of National Revenue made that fact known in the house previously. I say there is an example of very great benefit having been achieved by the mere enactment of that legislation.
I say without fear of successful contradiction that that statement is not accurate, that it is in fact not in accord with the facts at all. I have taken the trouble to have the legislation of 1958 examined. The legislation of 1958 repealed all the old legislation and substituted new legislation in its place. The new legislation is the law. The old legislation is not the law, and if the Minister of National Revenue has not been administering the new legislation he has not been carrying out the law. I am not inclined to believe that that is the case. I am told that there is only one respect in which the old law that was on the statute books before 1958 with respect to dumping is on the statute books at the present time, and that is the end of season clause that was enacted in 1955, I think.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Certainly.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. gentleman said he had had this examined. Would he mind telling the committee by whom he had it examined? He said "I was told", and would he mind telling the committee by whom he was told?

I had it examined by someone I thought had more knowledge of this subject than I. I examined it, myself, but I thought I should have my opinion verified by someone. If I am wrong, then the hon. member for Carleton, being learned in the law and not needing any help as I do, can show me in what respects I am wrong.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Would it have been Grant Dexter?

No, I do not regard Grant Dexter as being a gentleman any more learned in the law than I am. The hon. gentleman, if he wants to go on with this quiz game, perhaps could go on with it outside of the house.
The fact of the matter is that it was stated repeatedly in this house by the Minister of National Revenue, and was confirmed the

other day by the Minister of Finance, that the change in the law with respect to dumping has never been enforced. Well, either the old law has been used, though it is no longer the law or the new law must have been used because the old law is no longer there. If that is the kind of information we are given about the administration of the law, then in heaven's name what can we expect if this legislation becomes law? The Minister of National Revenue would be given the freedom under this legislation to impose a lower tariff or a higher tariff at his whim upon any kind of commodity that, by any stretch of the imagination-it will only be by imagination-can be said to be made in Canada.
I think I can demonstrate very easily and very quickly that it would be quite impos-sibie, under this legislation, to take any kind of meaningful appeal at all. I am thinking of shelf goods, and all the things that have to be determined on an appeal. It has to be determined on appeal, first of all, that the article which it is proposed to import is of approximately the same class or kind as the goods produced in Canada.
What does that mean?

The minister must determine, at some stage, what the normal consumption is of this particular article which presumably is not exactly but only approximately the same as something else made in Canada. It has to be determined what the range of these things is that are approximately alike, and until the tariff board has decided what these things are, how in heaven's name is the minister or anyone else going to decide what normal Canadian consumption is?
I admit this is a very difficult matter, but how can you determine what the normal consumption is of something until you know what that something is? Once you put in the word "approximately", you have got to have someone say what are these things that are approximately like the thing someone is seeking to import. For that reason it seems to me it would be quite impossible, even if the minister wanted an appeal to be taken on all these other things, to get a stated case on which to appeal.
I should like to ask the minister how these things will be dealt with in the future. When an importer seeks to import an article will the minister determine the normal Canadian consumption first before the appeal is taken so that at least the importer will be told what the normal Canadian consumption is supposed to be, and so that he knows the set of facts upon which he may base his appeal? How can he be told that if the minister does not know what the goods are?

According to the Minister of Finance it would be possible to appeal to the board to find out whether these goods were approximately of a class or kind made in Canada. Would you determine the normal consumption in Canada of an unknown article before the appeal is taken, or would the appeal be taken first in order to determine whether this article is approximately the same? After that appeal is taken would one go back to the Minister of National Revenue and have him determine, after the tariff board has said what are the things that are approximately alike, what the normal quantity is? Is that the way this thing is going to be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Now you are
labouring this heavily.
The minister is the one now making suggestions that these practical, concrete questions do not deserve to be answered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Not at all, I am just pointing out how the hon. gentleman is labouring this subject. The hon. gentleman is obviously in labour trying to keep it going until six o'clock.
I should like to ask you, sir, to suggest to the Minister of Finance that he cease imputing motives to others. I have plenty to say about this thing.
So has the public.

So has the public, as my hon. friend from Kenora-Rainy River points out. I have plenty to say about this. I have had a good deal of difficulty in selecting which of the many points I would start to speak about this afternoon. I chose to speak about this particular subject because it is very complicated and it seemed to me it would be only reasonable to give the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue time to marshal their facts in order to explain how this would be done.
